title: RealAether impact and solar timeline
timezone_note: Civil dates are in the usual historical (Gregorian/Julian as commonly cited) calendar. Instrumental Dst times are UT from NASA OMNI2 / Kyoto WDC, as used in our Part 2 study.
license: Code MIT · Data & charts CC BY 4.0, credit RealAether (Geebs369)
methods: Craters of the last ~100,000 years, plus a few famous older structures, are taken from the Earth Impact Database as compiled on Wikipedia’s List of impact structures on Earth (the PASSC / passc.net database site was down when this page was built). Historical airbursts and falls are entered only when they are widely documented; Ch’ing-yang is marked unverified. Solar-particle (Miyake) events and geomagnetic storms follow our 27 November 2026 cataclysm study, which used NASA OMNI2 Dst, Kyoto WDC, SILSO sunspot numbers, and NOAA SWPC. Lunar flashes and Encke node crossings come from our Taurid and monument–sky studies. Evidence labels: confirmed = widely accepted with physical or instrumental records; debated = a real event or structure whose cause, age, or interpretation is disputed; unverified = a historical claim without confirming physical evidence; model = a calculated orbital-geometry epoch, not a dated impact.

events.title: Younger Dryas boundary — impact trigger?
events.place: global climate event; claimed North American impact
events.summary: The Younger Dryas was a sudden Northern Hemisphere cold snap in the middle of the warming that ended the last ice age, not the end of the ice age itself. A proposed impact or airburst trigger (the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, supported in public by Randall Carlson among others) is probably not the cause: our review puts confidence at about 85% against. There is no crater of the right age, the nanodiamond, platinum and melt-glass evidence is disputed, and our Taurid / Encke node-crossing test is neutral (nearest crossing 649 years away; a random date does as well, p ≈ 0.53). Meltwater from glacial Lake Agassiz weakening Atlantic overturning is the better-supported explanation. A small airburst cannot be completely ruled out.

citations.text: RealAether Monument–sky study (Impact Hypothesis, Part 3), 27 Nov 2026
Encke node-crossing test: nearest crossing 649 yr from the YDB, p(random date as close) = 0.54

events.title: Encke node crossing (inbound, descending)
events.summary: Calculated epoch when comet Encke’s descending node is Earth-crossing (inbound). Our N-body backtrack finds 10 such crossings in the last ~14,000 years, coming in pairs about 300 years apart with a mean period of about 2,930 years. These are orbital-geometry results, not dated impacts. Clone-cloud spread grows for older crossings (centuries at the earliest pairs; decades for the most recent).

citations.text: RealAether Taurid / Encke study (Impact Hypothesis, Phases 2–4), 27 Nov 2026; encke_node_crossings.json

events.title: Miyake event, 7176 BC
events.summary: A confirmed extreme solar-particle event: a sharp, nearly global spike in radiocarbon (¹⁴C) and beryllium-10 (¹⁰Be). Events like this do not burn the land; before the electrical age the main human effect would have been great auroras. They recur at ordinary solar-activity levels, with a lower-bound rate of about 2–10% per century.

citations.text: Confirmed Holocene Miyake events as compiled in RealAether cataclysm study (Part 2), 27 Nov 2026

events.title: Miyake event, AD 774/5
events.summary: The strongest confirmed Miyake event of the Holocene, first identified as a rapid ¹⁴C rise in Japanese cedar rings and later confirmed in ¹⁰Be ice-core records. Models find only modest ozone loss and no significant climate effect; the ground-level radiation dose was small. Chronicles of unusual auroras are the main human record.

events.title: Ch’ing-yang stone shower
events.summary: Ming-era and later Chinese chronicles describe a shower of stones said to have killed thousands. The reports are often cited, but the event is not confirmed by a crater, meteorites in hand, or a modern critical study that would put it on the same footing as Tunguska or Chelyabinsk.

citations.text: Often cited from later compilations of Chinese historical meteor records (e.g. Yau, Weissman & Yeomans 1994, Meteoritics 29:864). Marked unverified on this page.

events.title: Tunguska
events.size: airburst, roughly 50–60 m object; ~2,150 km² of forest flattened
events.summary: The largest impact event in recorded history: an object roughly 50–60 m across exploded in the air over a remote region of Siberia and flattened about 80 million trees across some 2,150 km². Few or no deaths were confirmed. There is no crater of that event.

citations.text: Classic surveys of the 1908 Tunguska airburst; energy and size in the commonly cited 50–60 m / multi-megaton range (see also NASEM 2022 context in our Part 2 study)

events.title: Curuçá River (“Brazil’s Tunguska”)
events.summary: Newspaper and later accounts describe a possible airburst that scorched forest along the Curuçá River. Details are thin, and the event is much less well documented than Tunguska or Chelyabinsk.

citations.text: Later discussions of the 13 August 1930 Curuçá event (sometimes called “Brazil’s Tunguska”); documentation is sparse, so this page marks it debated

events.title: Sikhote-Alin
events.size: iron fall; more than 100 craters, the largest tens of metres
events.summary: A witnessed iron-meteorite fall. The meteoroid broke up in the atmosphere and rained down tons of fragments, leaving more than 100 small craters. It is a fall, not a city-scale airburst.

citations.text: Classic documentation of the 12 February 1947 Sikhote-Alin iron meteorite shower and crater field

events.title: Carancas
events.summary: A stony meteorite reached the ground and excavated a crater about 13 m across near a village. Some locals reported feeling sick afterward; a shock-heated, water-filled crater and arsenic-bearing sediments have been discussed as possible causes, rather than “meteorite poisoning.”

citations.text: Tancredi et al. and follow-up work on the 15 September 2007 Carancas crater, Peru (~13 m)

events.title: Chelyabinsk
events.size: ~20 m stony object; airburst ~440 kt TNT
events.summary: A rock about 20 m across entered over the southern Urals and exploded in the air. NASA’s official energy estimate is about 440 kilotons of TNT (roughly 30 times the Hiroshima bomb). The shock wave blew out windows across thousands of buildings and injured about 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass. It was not seen coming in advance.

citations.text: NASA / CNEOS fireball record; Brown et al. 2013, Nature 503:238; Popova et al. 2013, Science 342:1069
Our CNEOS window 1 Jan 2005–4 Oct 2026 includes Chelyabinsk; 81 fireballs ≥1 kt, 3.72 per year (RealAether Part 2)

events.title: Taurid lunar impact flashes
events.place: near side of the Moon (NELIOTA survey)
events.summary: The NELIOTA lunar impact-flash survey recorded 16 flashes from Taurid meteoroids on 29–31 October 2022, a year predicted in advance as a Taurid resonant-swarm return. Across August 2019–August 2023, flashes per observed hour were 1.84 times higher in October–November than in other months (p = 0.0005). Sporadic flashes show no such excess (p = 0.40). This is the one clear positive in our Taurid tests.

citations.text: Liakos et al. 2024 (NELIOTA); RealAether Taurid study, 27 Nov 2026

events.title: CNEOS fireballs ≥1 kt
events.summary: NASA CNEOS fireball data in our study window show 81 events of at least 1 kiloton, or 3.72 per year, with a power-law index of 0.98 (90% CI 0.82–1.20). That matches Brown et al. (2002) almost exactly (3.7 per year, index 0.90). The largest event in the window is about 441 kt (Chelyabinsk). This is a survey statistic, not a single impact.

citations.text: NASA CNEOS fireballs; RealAether cataclysm study (Part 2), future_risk.json, window 2005-01-01 to 2026-10-04
Brown et al. 2002, Nature 420:294

events.title: Carrington event
events.summary: The benchmark extreme geomagnetic storm of the instrumental era, following a white-light solar flare observed by Richard Carrington and Richard Hodgson on 1 September 1859. Telegraph systems sparked and shocked operators. Estimated Dst ranges from about −850 nT (low-end) to −1,760 nT. From the two or three Carrington-class storms since 1859, we estimate about 11–16% probability per decade (90% CI 2–37%).

citations.text: Carrington 1859; later Dst reconstructions compiled in our Part 2 study (low-end about −850 nT; mid-range often about −1,200 nT)
Riley 2012, Space Weather 10:S02012 (about 12% per decade)

events.title: February 1872 storm (probable Carrington-class)
events.summary: A severe 19th-century storm, probably of Carrington class according to Hayakawa et al. (2023). Counting it with 1859 and 1921 is what raises the per-decade odds from about 11% (two events) to about 16% (three events) in our Part 2 study.

citations.text: Hayakawa et al. 2023, as cited in RealAether cataclysm study (Part 2)

events.place: Québec, Canada, and the wider Earth system
events.summary: A severe geomagnetic storm that collapsed the Hydro-Québec grid, leaving about 6 million people without power for roughly nine hours. In the OMNI2 hourly Dst record we used (1963–2026), this is the strongest storm: Dst −589 nT on 14 March 1989 at 01:00. Kp reached 9.

events.place: Earth (including a Malmö, Sweden blackout and airline reroutes)
events.summary: A famous series of extreme solar eruptions near solar maximum of Cycle 23. Kp reached 9. In our OMNI2 record, Dst reached −383 nT on 30 October 2003 at 22:00. A Malmö blackout and airline reroutes are documented.

events.title: February 2022 Starlink loss

metrics.dst_nT: did not reach −100 nT in our OMNI2 ≤ −100 nT storm list

events.summary: A relatively modest geomagnetic storm — it does not appear among OMNI2 storms of Dst ≤ −100 nT in the 1963–2026 list we used — still led to the loss of 38 newly launched Starlink satellites, which re-entered after atmospheric density rose at their unusually low deployment altitude. It is a reminder that space systems can fail in storms well below Carrington or even Québec 1989 strength.

citations.text: SpaceX and NOAA accounts of the 3–4 February 2022 Starlink losses (38 satellites)
RealAether Part 2: the event is listed among documented technological harms; it is absent from our OMNI2 Dst ≤ −100 nT catalogue, so the storm was weaker than that threshold

events.title: Gannon storm
events.place: Earth (G5 level; GPS disruption to farm equipment among the effects)
events.summary: The first G5 (extreme) geomagnetic storm of Solar Cycle 25, often called the Gannon storm. In our OMNI2 record, Dst reached −406 nT on 11 May 2024 at 02:00, the third-strongest storm in the 1963–2026 hourly list after March 1989 and 20 November 2003. Kp reached 9. Documented effects included GPS disruption to farm equipment. We found no deaths attributed to the storm.

citations.text: NASA OMNI2 / Kyoto WDC Dst: −406 nT at 2024-05-11 02:00; NOAA SWPC Kp = 9, G5

events.title: Solar Cycle 25 maximum
events.summary: NASA, NOAA and the Solar Cycle Prediction Panel announced on 15 October 2024 that the Sun had entered the solar-maximum period of Cycle 25, noting that the exact peak month would be identified only later. SILSO later placed the 13-month smoothed sunspot-number maximum in October 2024 at 160.9 — stronger than the 2019 panel’s midpoint forecast of 115. By April 2026 the smoothed number had fallen to 88.6. NOAA SWPC has projected a minimum around December 2030.
